label: Ascent Stage Crew Cabin & Cockpit

specs.material: Welded 2219 aluminum alloy pressure vessel with Inconel heat foil

function: Pressurized cabin for Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin. Integrated the Apollo Guidance Computer (AGC), Primary Guidance Navigation and Control System (PGNCS), triangular forward windows, overhead docking tunnel, and 16 reaction control system (RCS) thrusters.
missionFacts: No pilot seats to minimize weight — astronauts stood throughout descent and ascent held by bungee restraints
The Ascent Engine burned Aerozine-50/NTO at 3,500 lbf constant thrust to reach lunar orbit on July 21, 1969
Docked with Command Module Columbia after 21 hours and 36 minutes on the lunar surface
Jettisoned in lunar orbit; eventually crashed into an unknown lunar impact site

label: LM Descent Stage Chassis & Propellant Tanks
function: Octagonal aluminum-alloy structural framework containing four large hypergolic propellant tanks, helium pressurization tanks, scientific equipment stowage bays (MESA), and the descent propulsion system.
missionFacts: Housed the Modular Equipment Stowage Assembly (MESA) containing the black-and-white TV camera
Gold Kapton thermal foil shielded against extreme lunar vacuum temperatures from -130 °C to +120 °C
Served as the launch platform when Eagle's ascent stage lifted off from Tranquility Base
Remains permanently in situ at Tranquility Base (0.67408° N, 23.47297° E)

label: Cantilever Struts & Regolith Footpads

specs.span: 9.45 m diagonal footprint across dish pads
specs.energy_absorption: Crushable aluminum honeycomb cartridges (up to 81 cm stroke)
specs.contact_probe_length: 1.73 m feeler wire probes on 3 footpads

function: Four deployable truss assemblies that dissipated touchdown kinetic energy without bouncing or tipping. Feeler probes touched lunar soil first, illuminating the blue 'CONTACT LIGHT' on the cockpit console.
missionFacts: "Contact light! OK, engine stop." — reported by Buzz Aldrin at 20:17:40 UTC, July 20, 1969
Touchdown was so gentle that the crushable honeycomb barely compressed, leaving the ladder higher than expected
Armstrong had to take a 1-meter jump from the final ladder rung to the footpad dish
Landing gear remains permanently deployed on the Moon, visible in LRO satellite photography

label: Descent Propulsion System (DPS Gimbaled Nozzle)

specs.propellants: Aerozine-50 and N2O4 hypergolic (no spark plugs needed)

function: World's first deeply throttleable rocket engine used in crewed flight. Allowed Neil Armstrong to slow down from orbital speed, hover, translate horizontally, and manually maneuver past a dangerous crater filled with boulders.
missionFacts: Armstrong manually extended the landing approach by ~40 seconds looking for smooth ground
Landed with approximately 25 to 30 seconds of descent propellant remaining
Engine nozzle was shut down just before touchdown so reflected exhaust wouldn't overpressure the base
Manufactured by TRW Systems Group (Redondo Beach, California)

label: Forward Egress Hatch & Crew Ladder

specs.hatch_dimensions: 81 cm × 81 cm (32 in × 32 in) square with rounded corners
specs.ladder_length: 9 tubular aluminum rungs on forward landing strut
specs.porch: Small exterior platform outside hatch for astronaut egress in bulky PLSS spacesuits

function: Egress hatch and ladder mounted to the forward landing strut (+Z axis). Enabled the astronauts to crawl backwards onto the exterior porch and descend to the lunar surface.
missionFacts: Neil Armstrong stepped off this ladder onto the lunar surface at 02:56 UTC on July 21, 1969
Mounted between the ladder rungs was the commemorative stainless steel Apollo 11 lunar plaque
Plaque inscription: "Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind."
Armstrong pulled a lanyard on this ladder to deploy the Westinghouse lunar television camera

label: S-Band Steerable High-Gain Antenna & Upper Deck
function: Parabolic steerable antenna transmitting live lunar surface television broadcasts, voice, biomedical telemetry, and telemetry across 384,400 km directly to the NASA Deep Space Network.
missionFacts: Beamed the historic live moonwalk broadcast watched by an estimated 650 million people worldwide
Signals were received simultaneously at Parkes Observatory (Australia), Goldstone (California), and Honeysuckle Creek
Allowed Houston flight controllers to monitor crew heart rates, oxygen levels, and LM system status
Required precise pointing at Earth as the planet moved across the lunar sky
